oneSentence: A United Nations-led process for bringing governments and other relevant actors together to discuss shared approaches for managing AI across borders.
plainExplanation:
This term refers to an international discussion process about how AI should be governed. Governance means the rules, institutions, practices and oversight used to guide how AI is developed and used. “Global” matters because AI systems, companies, data flows and technical standards often cross borders.

What goes in? Different countries, UN bodies, experts, companies and civil society groups bring concerns, evidence and proposals. They may discuss safety, human rights, development, interoperability, accountability and capacity-building, which means helping countries build the skills and systems they need.

What happens? Meetings, consultations, reports and negotiations help participants compare priorities and look for common ground. Sometimes the process is mainly for dialogue and agenda-setting. Sometimes it supports later outputs such as recommendations, principles, resolutions or other normative instruments, meaning texts that guide behaviour or set expectations.

What comes out? Not always a binding rule. Often the output is shared language, clearer problem definitions, areas of agreement, and a basis for future action in national, regional or international forums. It is often confused with one specific panel or one negotiation text, but the dialogue is broader: it is the conversation space and process, not only one document or one expert body.

everydayAnalogy.title: A library network choosing shared rules for document recommendations
everydayAnalogy.story: Libraries in Nairobi, São Paulo, Bangkok and Amman all use software to recommend documents from their catalogues. Each library has different readers, languages and laws, so they meet to discuss what the software should and should not do. One library worries about bias against local-language materials, another worries about privacy, and another needs simple systems because staff and budgets are limited. They do not leave the meeting with one perfect machine for everyone, but they do agree on shared principles, common questions to test, and a plan for future coordination.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A library network is much smaller and simpler than global AI governance. In real international dialogue, participants may have conflicting legal systems, strategic interests and unequal technical capacity. Also, the global dialogue can influence later UN texts, standards and national policies, while the library meeting mainly affects one service.

visual.title: How a global dialogue on AI governance moves from concerns to shared next steps
visual.learningObjective: Show that the dialogue is a process: issues are raised, discussed across groups, and may lead to shared language or later policy work, not instant global rules.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with five boxes. Read from concerns entering the process to possible outputs. Arrows show that each step builds on the previous one, but the final box lists several possible outcomes rather than a single result.

steps.label: 1. Issues raised
steps.explanation: Countries and other participants bring problems, evidence and priorities such as safety, inclusion, development or accountability.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with small input icons: speech bubbles, a document, a shield and a globe. Label inputs from governments, experts, industry and civil society.

steps.label: 2. Dialogue organised
steps.explanation: The UN or another agreed forum structures meetings, consultations or reports so participants can compare views.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a calendar and meeting table. Add a small label: consultations, meetings, reports.

steps.label: 3. Differences examined
steps.explanation: Participants identify where views align and where they differ, including legal, technical and development concerns.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with two overlapping circles and coloured notes marked agreement and difference.

steps.label: 4. Common ground shaped
steps.explanation: Shared terms, principles or options are drafted, even if some issues remain unsettled.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a draft document and highlighted lines. Add a small note: not necessarily binding.

steps.label: 5. Next steps
steps.explanation: The process may inform resolutions, standards, capacity-building or later negotiations in other forums.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box splitting into three small outputs: policy text, standards checklist and training/capacity icon.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal a short example of what might happen there, with the arrow path highlighted.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains the process behind a global dialogue on AI governance in five steps. First, participants such as governments, experts, companies and civil society bring concerns and evidence about AI. Second, an international forum organises meetings, consultations or reports. Third, participants compare positions and identify both agreements and disagreements. Fourth, they draft shared language, principles or options, though these may not be binding. Fifth, the dialogue may feed into later outputs such as resolutions, standards work or capacity-building. The main message is that the dialogue is a staged process that helps build common ground rather than an instant world law.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-step horizontal diagram with numbered boxes and arrows. Each box includes a short label and one icon. Expanded text for each step appears below the diagram instead of using hover or animation.

workedExample.scenario: A UN meeting gathers 42 countries, 6 international organisations, 12 companies, 15 academic experts and 18 civil society groups to discuss AI in public services.
workedExample.input: Participants submit short notes before the meeting. Common topics include transparency, testing, language inclusion, energy use and support for lower-capacity countries.
process: The secretariat groups the submissions into five themes and circulates a summary note.
In the meeting, participants discuss where views already overlap, such as the need for human oversight in high-impact uses.
They identify open questions, including whether voluntary guidance is enough or whether stronger regulation will be needed in some areas.
A chair's summary records points of convergence and lists practical follow-up work on standards, capacity-building and future negotiations.
workedExample.result: No single treaty is adopted, but the dialogue produces shared vocabulary, a public summary of priorities, and a clearer basis for later UN and national work.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN team reviewing programme monitoring data wants to brief delegates on how AI tools might support analysis across countries without creating harm or exclusion.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The global dialogue helps frame what questions to ask beyond technical performance, including fairness, accountability, interoperability and whether all Member States can participate in shaping the rules.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only approved systems and properly governed datasets. Do not place personal, confidential or protection-sensitive programme information into a public AI service for drafting or analysis.

whyItMatters: A non-specialist may hear this term in news, UN documents or policy debates and assume it means a single global law is coming. Usually it means something more practical: a structured international effort to compare risks, values and options before rules or standards are set. That matters because the way these discussions are framed can shape whose concerns count, which problems get priority, and whether smaller or lower-capacity countries can influence outcomes. It also affects whether future AI rules work across borders or clash with each other.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It means the world has already agreed on one set of AI rules.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A dialogue is a process for discussion and coordination. It may lead to shared principles or later negotiations, but it does not by itself create one binding global rulebook.

Governments are central in intergovernmental settings, but many discussions also involve experts, civil society, companies and technical bodies. Exactly who participates depends on the forum and mandate.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It is the same thing as the UN scientific panel on AI.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The scientific panel is a specific body focused on evidence and analysis. The global dialogue is broader and refers to the wider international discussion and coordination process around AI governance.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is the international conversation about how AI should be guided and overseen so countries can handle shared problems together.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In more precise terms, this is a UN-linked or multilateral process for agenda-setting, consultation and possible norm-shaping on AI across jurisdictions. Inputs can include Member State positions, expert evidence, stakeholder submissions and Secretariat support. Through meetings, reports and negotiations, participants identify convergences, disagreements and possible frameworks for cooperation. Outputs may include political guidance, resolutions, elements of normative instruments, coordination on standards, capacity-building priorities or pathways for future negotiation. The term does not automatically imply a binding treaty, a single institution or consensus on all substantive issues.

keyTakeaway: Think of it as the international process for building common ground on AI governance, not as a single law, meeting or expert panel.

quickCheck.question: Which description best fits a global dialogue on AI governance?
options: A process where countries and other relevant actors discuss shared approaches to AI across borders
A binding global treaty that automatically applies to every AI system
A single expert panel that alone writes all international AI rules
A technical method for training AI models on data from many countries
quickCheck.explanation: The term refers to a discussion and coordination process. It can inform later treaties, resolutions, standards or panels, but it is not itself any one of those things.
